newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu tangles with Orthodox partners on ruling.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu tangles with Orthodox partners on ruling.

text.p: A court ruling granting an Israeli woman from the Reform Jewish movement access to a bastion of Jewish Orthodoxy has locked Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a tangle with religious coalition partners.

Netanyahu took over the powers of his religious affairs minister Eli Suissa late on Tuesday to appoint Dr Joyce Brenner to a religious local council after Suissa, of the Orthodox Shas party, had refused to do so.
Israel's High Court ruled last week that authorities had to give Brenner a seat on the council, which provides religious services to residents of the city of Netanya.
Orthodox legislators in Netanyahu's government vowed to pass a law bypassing the court decision. One lawmaker said he was considering resigning.

"It's not even necessary to explain the damage this will cause to the whole issue of Judaism and the Jewish state. I feel I am unable to continue participating in such a coalition," said parliament member Moshe Gafni of the Torah Judaism party.
According to the court decision, the religious affairs minister had until midnight on Tuesday to publish the appointment in the government's official gazette.

"Prime Minister Netanyahu appointed himself religious affairs minister and published a notice in the official gazette about Dr Brenner's appointment to the Netanya religious council in line with the High Court ruling," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
Suissa said Netanyahu promised to return him to the post within days.

"We will correct the law and everything will go back to normal. We will live our lives and we won't allow a group that doesn't even exist to disrupt life in Israel," said Orthodox lawmaker Avraham Ravitz.
The religious affairs ministry and municipal authorities are authorised to appoint people to religious councils operating in Israeli cities and towns.
Members of the councils have always been Orthodox, the most religiously stringent of Jewish streams and the dominant one in Israel but not abroad.
Israel's Orthodox clergy has a near monopoly over the state's religious institutions, fighting to prevent the Reform and Conservative movements from gaining footholds.
Orthodox hegemony in Israel has outraged Jews in the United States, where the Reform movement is widespread.
